findings.problem: LedgerWorkflow uses pub status: String, pub is_validated: bool, pub is_sent: bool — any combination is constructible, including invalid ones like status='sent' with is_sent=false, or status='deleted' with is_sent=true. There is no enforced invariant between status and the boolean flags.
findings.failure_mode: Downstream code cannot assume status/flag consistency; bugs silently produce inconsistent ledger records that may pass through without detection, violating DDD invariants and making the state machine unrecoverable.
findings.fix: Replace status: String with an enum (e.g., enum LedgerStatus { New, Validated, Sent, Failed }) and remove is_sent/is_validated bools. Encode transitions as methods on the enum or a typestate struct that makes illegal states unconstructible.

findings.problem: is_validated: bool is a primitive boolean lifecycle flag. This is explicitly forbidden by the pre-commit safety audit — bool fields that encode state must be replaced with enums or typestates.
findings.failure_mode: Boolean flags can be set independently of other fields, creating inconsistent states. A ledger can appear both validated and unvalidated depending on which field is queried, leading to incorrect processing decisions.
findings.fix: Replace is_validated: bool and is_sent: bool with a single status enum that encodes the full lifecycle. The status enum itself is the single source of truth.

findings.problem: status: String allows arbitrary string values ('sent', 'SENT', 'pending', 'foobar', '') that have no domain meaning. This is a primitive obsession — a string should not represent a typed domain concept.
findings.failure_mode: Typo in status comparison ('Sent' vs 'sent'), case-sensitivity bugs, and arbitrary invalid values all cause silent misrouting. String comparison is error-prone and unenforceable at compile time.
findings.fix: Replace with a sealed enum: enum LedgerStatus { New, Validated, Sent, Failed }. Use match/arm-based dispatch instead of string comparison.

findings.problem: mark_sent blindly sets status='sent' and is_sent=true regardless of the current state. There is no precondition check — a ledger in any state (including 'deleted' or 'failed') can be marked sent. This violates state-machine invariants.
findings.failure_mode: Invalid state transitions (e.g., deleted → sent, failed → sent) produce incorrect ledger records. In an audit system, this breaks the immutability and traceability guarantees of the ledger.
findings.fix: Replace with a fallible method on a typed state machine: fn mark_sent(self) -> Result<LedgerStatusSent, TransitionError> that only accepts transitions from Validated → Sent. Use the typestate pattern to enforce legal transitions at compile time.

findings.problem: LedgerWorkflow is a mutable data bag with pub fields and no encapsulation. mark_sent mutates the struct in place. The domain logic (what states are valid, how transitions work) is encoded as free functions rather than being embedded in the type.
findings.failure_mode: No compile-time guarantee that transitions are legal. Any caller can construct LedgerWorkflow with arbitrary field combinations. The core is not a pure domain model — it is a mutable record with no invariants.
findings.fix: Make fields private, provide a fallible constructor that establishes invariants, and encode transitions as methods on a typestate or enum that guarantees legal state machines.

findings.problem: mark_sent returns LedgerWorkflow directly with no error type. Invalid transitions are silently accepted rather than reported as typed domain errors.
findings.failure_mode: Callers have no way to distinguish a successful transition from a no-op or invalid one. Error handling is impossible without inspecting internal fields, breaking the railway-oriented error model.
findings.fix: Return Result<LedgerWorkflow, TransitionError> where TransitionError is a typed enum (e.g., enum TransitionError { InvalidState, AlreadySent }). Parse at boundaries into trusted types; reject invalid transitions explicitly.

missing_evidence: no benchmark exists — the crate has no benchmarks for transition throughput or state-machine performance
no profiler data — no allocation profiles or hot-path analysis for mark_sent or any lifecycle method
no allocation evidence — no measured budget for Vec/String allocations in the workflow pipeline
no second-ring evidence — no integration or end-to-end tests exercising the full state machine
no command evidence — no cargo test / cargo clippy output confirming compilation or correctness
residual_risk: The LedgerWorkflow struct is a primitive-dbag anti-pattern with no type discipline, no state machine invariants, and no error handling. All 6 Holzman rules are violated. The code as written represents an invalid-state-permitting data structure with no functional core — it must be refactored with enums/typestates before any delivery.
